summary.text: For \(n=9\), the product of the first nine primes is \(223092870\), and the resulting value factors as \(49770428644836901=29^2\cdot53\cdot1116604864937\). Thus it is divisible by the square of the prime \(29\), so it is not squarefree and the conjunction fails.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
p_0=2,\quad p_1=3,\quad p_2=5,\quad p_3=7,\ldots
\]
denote the primes in increasing order, and define the primorial
\[
P_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}p_k.
\]
The product is empty when \(n=0\), so \(P_0=1\). Thus the sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=P_n^2+1.
\]
In particular, this convention gives \(a(0)=2\), \(a(1)=5\), and so agrees with the stated offset-zero sequence.

We disprove the assertion that every \(a(n)\) is squarefree by considering \(n=9\). The first nine primes are
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23.
\]
Their product is
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_9
&=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19\cdot23\\
&=223{,}092{,}870.
\end{aligned}
\]
For completeness, this product can be accumulated as
\[
2\cdot3=6,\quad 6\cdot5=30,\quad 30\cdot7=210,
\]
\[
210\cdot11=2310,\quad 2310\cdot13=30030,
\]
\[
30030\cdot17=510510,\quad 510510\cdot19=9699690,
\]
and
\[
9699690\cdot23=223092870.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(9)
&=(223{,}092{,}870)^2+1\\
&=49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901.
\end{aligned}
\]
This integer has a repeated prime factor. More precisely,
\[
49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901
 =29^2\cdot59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661.
\]
Equivalently, displaying a little more of the factorization,
\[
a(9)=29^2\cdot53\cdot1{,}116{,}604{,}864{,}937,
\]
since
\[
53\cdot1{,}116{,}604{,}864{,}937
=59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661.
\]

The divisibility by \(29^2\) can also be seen directly with much smaller modular arithmetic. Since \(29^2=841\), we have
\[
223{,}092{,}870=841\cdot265{,}270+800,
\]
so
\[
P_9\equiv800\equiv-41\pmod{841}.
\]
It follows that
\[
P_9^2+1\equiv(-41)^2+1=1682=2\cdot841\equiv0\pmod{841}.
\]
Thus \(29^2\mid a(9)\), as the displayed exact factorization also shows.

It remains only to note that \(29\) is prime. Indeed, any composite positive integer has a prime divisor no greater than its square root. Since \(\sqrt{29}<6\), a composite \(29\) would have to be divisible by one of the primes \(2,3,5\). It is odd, its digit sum is \(11\) and hence it is not divisible by \(3\), and it does not end in \(0\) or \(5\). Therefore none of \(2,3,5\) divides it, and \(29\) is prime.

A positive integer is squarefree precisely when the square of no prime divides it. Because the prime square \(29^2\) divides \(a(9)\), the term \(a(9)\) is not squarefree. Hence the universal assertion
\[
\forall n\ge 0,\quad a(n)\text{ is squarefree}
\]
is false.

The proposed combined conjecture is the conjunction of that universal squarefreeness assertion with the assertion that \(a(n)\) is prime for infinitely many \(n\). A conjunction can hold only if each of its two parts holds. Its first part has just been contradicted by the explicit index \(n=9\). Therefore the conjunction is false, independently of whether the sequence contains infinitely many prime terms.
